title: Spontaneous Regression of a Large Vestibular Schwannoma: Is Nonoperative Management Reasonable?
content:
Vestibular schwannomas (VSs) are the most common cerebellopontine tumors. The natural history of smaller-sized VSs (<30 mm) has been well-studied, leading to the recommendation of a “watch and wait” approach. However, large VSs (>30 mm) have not been extensively studied, mainly because of their rarity. As such, most patients are conventionally offered surgery which carries a significant risk of neurological morbidity. Here, we report a case of a giant VS (>40 mm) in a 30-year-old man who regressed spontaneously. He was lost to follow-up for 18 years and, upon re-presentation, the symptomatology drastically improved and repeat imaging demonstrated a marked reduction in tumor size. Referring to similar cases in other studies, we postulate that most large and giant VSs undergo a phase of growth and stasis, followed by regression due to shifts in the balance between tumorigenic and regressive factors. Taken together with emerging molecular data, further studies are required to better understand the history of large and giant VSs to shape more personalized treatment options. This potentially includes non-operative management as a tenable option.

INTRODUCTIONVestibular schwannoma (VS) is the most common cerebellopontine angle (CPA) tumor in adults, accounting for 8% of all intracranial tumors and more than 80% of all CPA tumors [1]. VS is classically thought to be benign, slow growing, and arises from myelinating Schwann cells of the both superior and inferior vestibular nerves [23]. The management of VS is complex and multi-faceted, varying largely between practitioners including in the decision to treat, choice of treatment modality, namely surgery (with variation in approaches including retro sigmoid, trans-labyrinthine, and middle fossa approaches) and radiation (stereotactic radiosurgery [SRS] or stereotactic radiotherapy) [4]. Today, there is no clear evidence supporting one treatment modality over another [5]. While patients should be offered a balanced view of the benefits and risks of each treatment option, this can be heavily subjected to each individual physician’s bias [6].The natural history of the disease is central to the discussion of the treatment options. Overall, the incidence of VS has been increasing from 0.72 per 100,000 person-years from 1995–1999 to 1.29 per 100,000 person-years from 2012–2016 [7]. Out of all the VS cases, 5% of them occur bilaterally, being associated with neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) [8]. However, the natural history of large (30–40 mm) and giant (>40 mm) sporadic unilateral tumors is elusive, given that they are uncommon, constituting 6% of newly diagnosed VS (equivalent to an incidence of 1 VS per million population per year) [9]. Even though these larger tumors were common in earlier studies, another factor to them not being studied well lies in the fact that a large proportion was operated on immediately [10]. This is contrasted to sporadic smaller-sized VS (<30 mm), for which more recent longitudinal studies have provided clarity on their natural history. Most of smaller-sized VS are slow growing, remain static in size, or are even known to regress since diagnosis, which has resulted in a shift of treatment recommendations heavily toward a ”watch-and-wait” approach. We report a case of giant sporadic VS that underwent spontaneous regression after 18 years of follow-up and summarize similar observations reported in recent years. We also discuss its implications for the management of large and giant VS, specifically, whether nonoperative management is a reasonable management option for most of this patient population.CASE REPORTWe present the case of a patient diagnosed with giant left VS (>40 mm) at 30 years of age who presented with episodic vertigo, left-sided hearing loss, and mild gait ataxia. MRI performed at another institution showed a giant VS (Fig. 1). The patient was lost to follow-up for 18 years. He subsequently presented again when he sought medical clearance for employment. Upon review, his vertigo episodes and ataxia were completely resolved, although he no longer had serviceable hearing on his left side. The clinical examination results were otherwise unremarkable for other neurological deficits. On repeat imaging, there was a >50% reduction in the overall tumor volume, with a significant reduction in the size of both the extrameatal and intrameatal components, along with a mass effect on the brainstem (Fig. 2). No hydrocephalus was observed. The patient was counseled and agreed to undergo regular follow-up for the tumor.DISCUSSIONPresentation of patients with large VSPatients with large or giant VS can present in two broad categories: 1) patients with debilitating clinical symptoms and signs attributable to brainstem compression (hearing loss, vertigo, nystagmus, cerebellar signs, lower cranial nerve palsies, or long tract signs), and/or intracranial hypertension with or without obstructive hydrocephalus (e.g., headache, vomiting, blurring of vision, papilledema), “significant” radiological brainstem compression and distortion of the fourth ventricle, and rarely when the patient presents in extremis after a tumor bleed; and 2) patients with minimal or no symptoms (“non-debilitating”). While the indications for surgical treatment are clear in the former group, the “watch-and-wait” approach is traditionally not recommended for the latter because of the possibility of life-threatening complications from tumor growth. In a large series of patients with VS who underwent surgical removal by Samii et al. [11], approximately a quarter (26%) of the patients with a large VS (defined as >40 mm) had clinical evidence of intracranial hypertension. Compared with smaller VS (<40 mm), the significant differences in the proportion of patients with neurological deficits were only found in gait ataxia, long tract signs, and lower cranial nerve dysfunction. Notably, the proportion of patients with the latter two neurological issues in the large VS group was low (approximately 10%). The pattern of neurological status among patients with large VS versus smaller-sized VS has also been observed in other similar studies [12131415]. In other words, the majority of patients with large VS without evidence of intracranial hypertension did not differ significantly in their neurological status and symptoms when compared to patients with smaller VS.Risk–benefit of various treatment modalitiesThere is no existing equipoise within the neurosurgical community regarding whether large or giant VSs should be treated. Coupled with the relative rarity of these tumors, no high-quality randomized controlled trials have compared the natural history of large VS (>3 cm) with the treatment outcomes of various modalities. Most, if not all, patients with large and giant VS undergo surgical treatment, particularly after the introduction of microsurgery in the field of neurosurgery, which has made VS excision safer. Gross total resection (GTR) or near total resection can frequently be achieved using well-established microsurgical techniques and neuromonitoring [5]. Despite this, surgical treatment continues to carry significant morbidity risks that notably increase with increasing tumor size. The risks are significantly increased to induce hearing loss (if there was serviceable hearing preoperatively) and facial nerve palsy (House-Brackmann grade III or poorer) of approximately 50% for tumors >40 mm in diameter in the setting of GTR and postoperative hematoma compared to smaller sized tumors [11]. There are other risks associated with any form of cranial surgery that are relatively small but not trivial, such as cerebellar edema, seizures, cerebrospinal fluid leakage, and infection of up to 8% overall.Given the profoundly negative impact on quality of life (QoL) from facial nerve deficits, recent expert consensus has advocated for the goal of VS management to be shifted away from GTR per se, toward “maintaining or improving QoL making every attempt at neurological function preservation with an acceptable oncological control” [16]. To this end, a planned or unplanned subtotal resection (STR) strategy to preserve facial nerve function during the surgical treatment for large and giant VS with postoperative radiation has been shown to produce excellent functional outcomes [17]. Interestingly, while tumor recurrence rates in GTR are extremely low (<10%), recurrence rates ranging from 30%–80% have been reported for patients who undergo STR of large and giant VS. Notably, several QoL studies have demonstrated a lower overall QoL for patients who have undergone surgical treatment compared to noninvasive options, including active surveillance [18]. Standalone upfront radiation-based options are generally not advocated for large and giant VS given the risks of swelling and edema that can produce a further mass effect in the posterior fossa. However, a more recent systemic review suggests that upfront SRS with a marginal dose of 11 Gy to 13 Gy can be offered to patients with large VS with good tumor control rates (approximately 90%) and acceptable rates of facial palsy (approximately 3%) [19].Balancing treatment risks with natural history of diseaseTo adequately counsel patients on the risk-benefit of treatment options, clarity on the natural history of the disease is cardinal. In the context of neurosurgical practice, this often represents a trade-off between upfront risks of neurological morbidity that have a significant impact on the patient’s QoL versus the outlook of a disease’s impact on a patient’s neurological function over time. Existing epidemiological studies examining the natural history of VS have predominantly focused on smaller-sized VS (<30 mm). Although a very small number of large VS were included in some of these studies, there was no separate analysis of their natural history. Smaller-sized VS is generally a slow-growing entity, as approximately only one-third of the intra-meatal tumors and one-fifth of the extra-meatal increase in size within the first 5 years of diagnosis (no tumor growth occurred after the fifth year of observation), with a higher growth rate within the first year (mean of approximately 10 mm/year vs. 0.9 mm at the fourth year if growth is detected) [5]. Notably, the cutoff for the quantitative definition of growth (linear or volumetric methodologies) remains controversial, even among large extra-meatal tumors. Notwithstanding, this has shifted the treatment paradigm of smaller-sized VS toward a “watch-and-wait” approach, particularly if repeat imaging shows minimal or no growth of a newly diagnosed VS. To identify a sub-group of patients that may benefit from early treatment, several papers have also attempted to identify risk factors associated with tumor growth. This includes features such as filling of the internal auditory canal, cystic and/or hemorrhagic content within the tumor, a history of NF2, young age, and an extra-canalicular component of greater than 20 mm. Notably, patients who were younger at diagnosis tended to have a larger VS (mean, 23 mm for the <40 years age group and mean, 13 mm for the >70 years age group). However, the association between these factors is not strong and is not widely accepted as an established risk factor independently or collectively [20].On the other hand, a significant proportion of smaller-sized VS are known to remain static (30%–60%) in size or are even known to regress (up to 20%) since diagnosis [21]. Reddy et al. [22] retrospectively reviewed a cohort of 45 patients with medium VS (15–31 mm in diameter) over a median follow-up period of 3 years. Approximately 25% of the tumors grew, while 65% of the tumors remained static in size and just under 10% regressed in size. In other words, approximately 75% of tumors did not grow. The overall mean tumor growth was approximately 1.2 mm per year, and the growth rate among the tumors that grew varied between 2 mm and 6 mm per year. Approximately 40% of the cohort eventually underwent intervention, mostly because of tumor growth and patient choice. However, only one patient experienced “clinical worsening” necessitating surgery. The incidence of regression was noted to be double the rate for smaller VS (20%) [2324]. The authors concluded that, for medium VS, it is reasonable to offer an initial period of “watch-and-wait” as a management option, on top of interventions.Taken together, both small- and medium-sized VS that grow would do so in their initial phases of growth and the rate of growth is slow. Most of these tumors subsequently remain stable in size after the first few years of growth, and a sizeable proportion of them would even regress with time. The association between tumor size at diagnosis and its propensity for growth is weak, and rarely if ever grows after a long period of non-growth or even regression [25]. Therefore, it is certainly plausible that large and giant VS share a similar tumor biology to small and medium VS; that is, the majority of tumors could be expected to remain static, with a smaller but sizeable proportion regressing after not demonstrating any significant growth during the initial phases of observation.Over the past decade, a series of case reports have reported large and giant VS remaining static and indeed regressing over time. This occurred both in patients who had been lost to follow-up for a number of years before the observed regression on imaging, and in a couple who had been imaged annually and observed to have regressed over time. Timmer and Graamans [26] reported a large VS that remained static in size for >18 years and eventually started to regress toward the 22nd year of follow-up [26]. Following this, a series of case reports illustrating this phenomenon were also published. Table 1 summarizes these reports [27282930].Plausible mechanismsWhile there is much work done on the tumorigenesis of VS, the mechanisms driving tumor growth, and naturally tumor regression remain elusive [31]. Classically, the inactivation of tumor suppressor gene NF2 located on chromosome 22q12 or the loss of its functional product moesin-erzin-radxin-like protein (merlin) plays a central role in tumorigenesis of VS. NF2 patients have a single germline mutation that predisposes them to VS (“double-hit” hypothesis), while other factors such as epigenetic modifications (e.g., deoxyribonucleic acid [DNA] methylation) of the NF2 gene promoter can effectively lead to a somatic biallelic inactivation [32]. In brief, merlin binds to actin and stabilizes the cell membrane cytoskeleton, serves as a “checkpoint” for Schwann cell repair, facilitates contact inhibition of receptor-dependent promitogenic pathways, and negatively influences growth signaling pathways such as mTORC1, EGFR, and Ras/Rac. However, this genetic predisposition alone does not entirely account for tumor biology, as not all VS tumors harbor NF2 mutations. Based on single-cell ribonucleic acid (RNA) sequencing, differential expression of merlin-regulated genes may also result in differential pathogenicity of NF2 mutations [33]. Genes unrelated to NF2 such as HGF/c-MET; noncoding genomes (such as microRNAs and epigenetic mechanisms) have also been implicated in sporadic VS.In recent years, there has been increasing interest in the tumor microenvironment and its influence on tumor behavior. They can be broadly classified into cellular components (immune cells, fibroblasts, platelets, etc.) and non-cellular components (structural proteins [extracellular matrix, regulatory proteins] and communication molecules [cytokines, chemokines, growth factors, etc.]), for which many entities, including macrophages, cyclo-oxygenase, and VEGF, have been identified as key players in tumorigenesis. VEGF, which plays a central role in vasculogenesis and angiogenesis, has been a target of considerable success in NF2 patients. In a meta-analysis, bevacizumab was reported to cause partial regression or change in >90% (41% regression, 47% no change in size) of patients, with approximately 10% of patients eventually requiring surgical intervention [34]. Hearing was preserved (20%–30%) or improved (50%–60%) in approximately 80% of patients. Nevertheless, serious toxicities were associated with approximately 17% of the patients, and the use of this drug may involve substantial financial costs. The off-label use of bevacizumab in sporadic VS has also been reported to produce a good response (>60% tumor volume reduction with full hearing preservation). At a macroscopic level, various studies reporting the regression of medium and large VS have also postulated tumor growth size “outpacing” the vascular supply after an initial period of growth, resulting in no growth or regression of this benign tumor. An inflammatory microenvironment has been shown to be associated with higher rates of tumor progression (increased proportion of immune cells and inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1, IL-6, and TNF) which may be driven in part by systemic inflammation [35]. It also led us to speculate that any attempt at less than GTR could trigger a proinflammatory change in the tumor microenvironment postoperatively, accounting for a relatively high tumor progression rate after STR compared to GTR and even the natural growth rates of conservatively treated VS. A more recent multiplatform molecular analysis of surgically resected VS specimens using methylation and RNA profiling also revealed two robust subgroups (immunogenic and proliferative) with distinct tumor microenvironments [36]. Notably, this study noted that there were no postoperative recurrence or growth in the former group, unlike the latter group in a mean 5-year follow-up period.Taken together, we postulate that the cause of stasis and regression of VS could be the inability of genetic and epigenetic factors driving tumorigenesis and growth to sustain a tumor microenvironment beyond its initial growth for most sporadic VS, where some function of the merlin gene may be variably preserved. The observation of this occurring even in large or giant VS suggests that this “balance” that influences tumor growth holds true regardless of tumor size (Fig. 3). In a significant proportion of individuals where regression is observed, changes in the local tumor microenvironment due to tumor growth may serve as a conduit or trigger a proinflammatory or apoptotic cascade that drives dramatic reductions in tumor size [37].The phenomenon of spontaneous tumo” reg’ession has also been sparsely reported in meningiomas and gliomas [3839]. To this end, in patients with large and giant VS with no debilitating symptoms, it might be essential to counsel them on the option of the “watch-and-wait” approach given the possibility of cessation of growth and even regression over time. Given the inherent limitations of case reports, further prospective studies are needed to better characterize the natural history of large and giant VS.LimitationsOne of the limitations of this case report is the substantial gap in follow-up period impacting the confidence in attributing the improvement in symptoms and the observed reduction in tumor size to spontaneous regression. We leveraged this opportunity to review relevant literature which make similar observations and postulate mechanisms to it as well. However, analysing only case reports has its limitations. For instance, it is not possible to draw a causal link from a single uncontrolled observation. In addition, it is not possible to generalize the findings due to a lack of a representative population. This also means information regarding prevalence rates and ratios cannot be derived solely from case reports. This underlines the need for larger prospective studies including control groups which would serve to remove the likelihood of chance, bias, and confounders. Some of the details regarding possible inclusion criteria of such prospective studies are highlighted in the “Future work” section.Future workRegarding future prospective studies surrounding this subject, a screening protocol, based on MRI findings, needs to be included. The inclusion criteria should ensure that there is no substantial risk to the participants in having an MRI to assess volumetric growth. The authors preliminarily suggest the following criteria: patients should be aged between 18 and 70 years, patients should have been newly diagnosed with a unilateral VS less than 6 months ago, the maximal tumor diameter should be more or equal to 30 mm at the CPA and the patients should not present with any debilitating clinical symptoms and signs attributable to brainstem compression, intracranial hypertension with or without obstructive hydrocephalus, “significant” radiological brainstem compression and distortion of the fourth ventricle or with a tumor bleed. In addition, patients must also be able and willing to comply to a 3 monthly surveillance scan especially in the initial follow-up period. Patients will be excluded if there is personal history or family history of NF2 in a first degree relative.ConclusionWe report a case of spontaneous regression of a large VS and review several similar case reports published in recent years. Taken together with similar observations in a larger series of small- and medium-sized VSs, we postulate that most large and giant VSs similarly undergo a period of growth, followed by stasis, with a significant proportion undergoing regression. This could be driven by a shift in balance that weighs away from the predominant tumorigenic factors driving tumor growth toward the predominance of regressive factors. Further studies to elucidate the natural history of large and giant VS are essential to provide adequate counseling to patients who would otherwise be conventionally offered surgical treatment that carries a significant risk of neurological morbidity.

diagnosis.severity_description: giant (>40 mm) unilateral sporadic vestibular schwannoma
diagnosis.quality_of_life_impact: episodic vertigo, left-sided hearing loss, mild gait ataxia; later no serviceable hearing on the left
diagnosis.disease_duration_before_healing: 18 years (lost to follow-up for 18 years before re-presentation with reduced tumor size on imaging)
diagnosis.primary_site: left cerebellopontine angle / vestibular nerve (intrameatal and extrameatal components)

remission_outcome.time_to_remission_raw: 18 years (interval without follow-up before repeat imaging showed regression)
remission_outcome.verification_detail: Repeat imaging after 18 years demonstrated >50% reduction in overall tumor volume with significant reduction in extrameatal and intrameatal components; no hydrocephalus observed.
remission_outcome.follow_up_duration_raw: 18 years gap between initial MRI and repeat imaging; ongoing regular follow-up planned

validation.statistical_improbability_notes: Case report of a giant (>40 mm) vestibular schwannoma with >50% volumetric reduction after an 18-year interval without treatment; authors note the long follow-up gap limits confidence in attributing change solely to spontaneous regression.
validation.extraction_notes: Tumor regression is well-supported by before/after MRI description, but exact dates/years, absolute measurements, and volumetric values are not provided in the narrative excerpt; 18-year interval introduces uncertainty about timing and trajectory of regression.

analysis.case_summary: A 30-year-old man was diagnosed on MRI with a giant (>40 mm) left vestibular schwannoma causing vertigo, hearing loss, and mild gait ataxia. After being lost to follow-up for 18 years without reported treatment, he re-presented with symptom improvement and repeat MRI showed >50% reduction in tumor volume.
key_healing_factors: Spontaneous tumor regression documented on repeat MRI after long interval
unique_features: Giant vestibular schwannoma (>40 mm) with marked spontaneous regression
Very long gap in follow-up (18 years) with symptomatic improvement
analysis.analysis_notes: This is a benign intracranial tumor regression case rather than cancer; the narrative does not report psycho-spiritual interventions, lifestyle changes, or anomalous experiences. The timing/trajectory of regression cannot be precisely established due to the 18-year loss to follow-up.
